imc-2014-01.title: Parametrize the matrix
imc-2014-01.body:
Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}x&z\\z&y\end{pmatrix}$. The conditions are $x+y=a$ and $xy-z^2=b$. Then
$$(x-y)^2+4z^2=(x+y)^2-4xy+4z^2=a^2-4b .$$
Conversely, if $x+y=a$ and $(x-y)^2+4z^2=a^2-4b$, then $xy-z^2=\frac{(x+y)^2-(x-y)^2}{4}-z^2=b$. So the symmetric matrices with trace $a$ and determinant $b$ correspond bijectively to the points $(x-y,\,2z)$ of the circle $\{(s,t):s^2+t^2=a^2-4b\}$ (with $x=\frac{a+s}2$, $y=\frac{a-s}2$, $z=\frac t2$).

- If $a^2-4b<0$ there is no such matrix.
- If $a^2-4b>0$ the circle has infinitely many points, so there are infinitely many matrices.
- If $a^2-4b=0$ the only point is $(0,0)$: $x=y=\frac a2$, $z=0$, i.e. $M=\frac a2I$ is the unique matrix.

**Answer:** all pairs $(a,b)$ with $a^2=4b$. ∎

imc-2014-01.title: Eigenvalues
imc-2014-01.body:
$\operatorname{trace}M=a$ and $\det M=b$ hold iff the eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ of $M$ are the roots of $t^2-at+b$. A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues, so we need $a^2\ge4b$.

If $\lambda_1\ne\lambda_2$, both $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ and $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_2,\lambda_1)$ work, so $M$ is not unique. Hence uniqueness forces $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda=\frac a2$, i.e. $a^2=4b$.

Conversely, if $a^2=4b$, any such $M$ is symmetric, hence orthogonally diagonalizable, with both eigenvalues $\lambda$: $M=Q^T(\lambda I)Q=\lambda I$. So $M=\frac a2 I$ is unique.

**Answer:** $a^2=4b$. ∎

imc-2014-02.title: Look at the ends of the blocks, then squeeze
imc-2014-02.body:
The sequence consists of blocks $1,2,\dots,m$ for $m=1,2,3,\dots$; block $m$ ends at position $T_m=\frac{m(m+1)}2$. Let $S(N)=\sum_{k=1}^Na_k$. Then
$$S(T_m)=\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{j(j+1)}2=\frac{m(m+1)(m+2)}6 .$$

**Necessity.** Along the subsequence $N=T_m$,
$$\frac{S(T_m)}{T_m^{\alpha}}=\frac{m(m+1)(m+2)/6}{\big(m(m+1)/2\big)^{\alpha}}=\frac{2^\alpha}{6}\,m^{3-2\alpha}\cdot\frac{(1+\frac1m)(1+\frac2m)}{(1+\frac1m)^{\alpha}} .$$
This tends to $0$ if $\alpha>\frac32$, to $\infty$ if $\alpha<\frac32$, and to $\frac{2^{3/2}}6=\frac{\sqrt2}3$ if $\alpha=\frac32$. Since $\beta$ must be positive and finite, necessarily $\alpha=\frac32$ and $\beta=\frac{\sqrt2}3$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $\alpha=\frac32$. For $T_m<N\le T_{m+1}$, monotonicity of $S$ (all $a_k>0$) gives
$$\frac{S(T_m)}{T_{m+1}^{3/2}}\le\frac{S(N)}{N^{3/2}}\le\frac{S(T_{m+1})}{T_m^{3/2}} .$$
The left side equals $\frac{S(T_m)}{T_m^{3/2}}\left(\frac{T_m}{T_{m+1}}\right)^{3/2}$ and the right side $\frac{S(T_{m+1})}{T_{m+1}^{3/2}}\left(\frac{T_{m+1}}{T_m}\right)^{3/2}$; since $T_{m+1}/T_m=\frac{m+2}{m}\to1$, both tend to $\frac{\sqrt2}3$. Hence $S(N)/N^{3/2}\to\frac{\sqrt2}3$.

**Answer:** $(\alpha,\beta)=\left(\frac32,\frac{\sqrt2}3\right)$. ∎

imc-2014-03.title: Induction by a small perturbation
imc-2014-03.body:
We induct on $n$. For $n=1$ take $a_1=a_0=1$: each $\pm x\pm1$ has one real root.

Suppose $a_0,\dots,a_n>0$ work for $n$. For a sign vector $\sigma$ let $P_\sigma(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n\sigma_ia_ix^i$; it has $n$ distinct real roots, all nonzero because $P_\sigma(0)=\pm a_0\ne0$. Hence
$$\tilde P_\sigma(x)=xP_\sigma(x)=\sigma_na_nx^{n+1}+\dots+\sigma_0a_0x$$
has $n+1$ distinct real roots $r_0<r_1<\dots<r_n$, all simple. By Rolle's theorem $\tilde P_\sigma'$ has a root in each interval $(r_{i-1},r_i)$; since $\deg\tilde P_\sigma'=n$, these are all its roots: $s_1<\dots<s_n$ with $r_{i-1}<s_i<r_i$. In particular $\tilde P_\sigma(s_i)\ne0$, and since $\tilde P_\sigma$ changes sign exactly at the simple roots $r_i$, the values $\tilde P_\sigma(s_1),\dots,\tilde P_\sigma(s_n)$ alternate in sign; moreover the sign of $\tilde P_\sigma$ near $-\infty$ is opposite to that at $s_1$ (one root $r_0$ in between), and the sign near $+\infty$ is opposite to that at $s_n$.

Choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than $|\tilde P_\sigma(s_i)|$ for all $2^{n+1}$ sign vectors $\sigma$ and all $i$. Every polynomial
$$R(x)=\pm a_nx^{n+1}\pm\dots\pm a_0x\pm\varepsilon$$
equals $\tilde P_\sigma(x)\pm\varepsilon$ for some $\sigma$. Then $R(s_i)$ has the same sign as $\tilde P_\sigma(s_i)$, and $R$ has the same sign as $\tilde P_\sigma$ near $\pm\infty$ (same leading term). So $R$ changes sign on each of the $n+1$ disjoint intervals $(-\infty,s_1),(s_1,s_2),\dots,(s_{n-1},s_n),(s_n,\infty)$, and by the intermediate value theorem has a root in each. As $\deg R=n+1$, it has exactly $n+1$ distinct real roots.

Thus $a'_{n+1}=a_n,\ a'_n=a_{n-1},\dots,a'_1=a_0,\ a'_0=\varepsilon$ work for $n+1$. ∎

imc-2014-04.title: A divisor of $1+p_1+\dots+p_1^{e_1}$
imc-2014-04.body:
Suppose $e_1$ is odd. By multiplicativity,
$$s(n)=\prod_{i=1}^k\left(1+p_i+\dots+p_i^{e_i}\right)=2n=2p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}.$$
The first factor has an even number $e_1+1$ of terms, so it equals $(1+p_1)(1+p_1^2+p_1^4+\dots+p_1^{e_1-1})$; hence $p_1+1\mid 2n$.

Since $p_1+1\ge3$ does not divide $2$, $\gcd(p_1+1,n)>1$, so some $p_j$ divides $p_1+1$. It is not $p_1$ (which does not divide $p_1+1$), so $p_j>p_1$, and $p_j\le p_1+1$; thus $p_j=p_1+1$. Two primes differing by $1$ must be $2$ and $3$: $p_1=2$, $p_j=3$, so $6\mid n$.

As $n>6$, the numbers $n,\frac n2,\frac n3,\frac n6,1$ are distinct divisors of $n$, so
$$s(n)\ge n+\frac n2+\frac n3+\frac n6+1=2n+1>2n,$$
a contradiction. Hence $e_1$ is even. ∎

*Remark.* For even $n$ this also follows from Euler's theorem that even perfect numbers are $2^{p-1}(2^p-1)$ with $2^p-1$ prime: here $e_1=p-1$, which is even because $n>6$ forces $p>2$.

imc-2014-05.title: Corners, heights and a cyclic sign argument
imc-2014-05.body:
Indices are taken modulo $3n$. Let $s_i$ denote the segment $A_iA_{i+1}$.

**Directions.** At each vertex the line turns left by $180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$. Hence $s_i$ has direction $e_{i\bmod3}$, where $e_0,e_1,e_2$ are unit vectors with $e_{c+1}$ obtained from $e_c$ by a $120^\circ$ counterclockwise rotation. Let $\nu_c$ be $e_c$ rotated by $90^\circ$ counterclockwise, and put
$$y_i=\nu_{i\bmod3}\cdot A_i\;\big(=\nu_{i\bmod 3}\cdot A_{i+1}\big),$$
the "height" of the line through $s_i$. If $i\ne j$, $i\equiv j\pmod3$, then $s_i,s_j$ are parallel, distinct, and not collinear (four vertices, no three collinear), so $y_i\ne y_j$; in particular parallel segments never meet.

**Corners.** Let $V_i=s_i\cup s_{i+1}$ (the corner at $A_{i+1}$), and let $c=i\bmod 3$. In the affine coordinates $f=\nu_c\cdot P$, $g=\nu_{c+1}\cdot P$ one computes $\nu_{c+1}\cdot e_c=\cos210^\circ<0$, $\nu_c\cdot e_{c+1}=\cos30^\circ>0$, $\nu_{c+1}\cdot e_{c+1}=\nu_c\cdot e_c=0$. So $A_{i+1}=(y_i,y_{i+1})$, the segment $s_i$ lies on the ray $\{f=y_i,\ g\ge y_{i+1}\}$ and $s_{i+1}$ on the ray $\{g=y_{i+1},\ f\ge y_i\}$: $V_i$ is part of the boundary of the quadrant $\{f\ge y_i,\ g\ge y_{i+1}\}$.

Take $j\ne i$ with $j\equiv i\pmod 3$ (same coordinates $f,g$). Since parallel segments do not meet, $V_i\cap V_j=(s_i\cap s_{j+1})\cup(s_j\cap s_{i+1})$. Now $s_i\cap s_{j+1}\neq\emptyset$ requires the point $(y_i,y_{j+1})$ to be on both rays: $y_i\ge y_j$ and $y_{j+1}\ge y_{i+1}$, i.e. (by distinctness) $y_i>y_j$ and $y_{i+1}<y_{j+1}$. Symmetrically $s_j\cap s_{i+1}\ne\emptyset$ requires $y_j>y_i$ and $y_{j+1}<y_{i+1}$. Consequently:
- at most one of the two intersections is nonempty;
- if one is nonempty, the pair is **discordant**: $(y_i-y_j)(y_{i+1}-y_{j+1})<0$.

**Every self-intersection is charged to a discordant pair.** Two non-adjacent segments that meet are non-parallel, so they are $s_a$ and $s_b$ with $b\equiv a+1\pmod 3$ (after possibly swapping names), and they meet in one point. Charge this crossing to the pair $\{a,b-1\}$; note $a\equiv b-1$, and $a\ne b-1$ since $s_a,s_{a+1}$ are adjacent. The crossing is $s_a\cap s_{(b-1)+1}$, so by the above each pair $\{i,j\}$ receives at most one crossing, and only if it is discordant. Hence
$$\#\text{self-intersections}\le\#\{\text{discordant pairs}\}=3\binom n2-\#\{\text{concordant pairs}\},$$
where the pairs are the $3\binom n2$ unordered pairs $\{i,j\}$, $i\ne j$, $i\equiv j\pmod 3$, and concordant means $(y_i-y_j)(y_{i+1}-y_{j+1})>0$.

**Reduction to one class.** Let $a_u=y_{3u}$ for $u\in\mathbb Z/n$ (distinct numbers). For $u\ne v$ consider the four signs
$$\sigma_c=\operatorname{sign}\big(y_{c+3u}-y_{c+3v}\big)\quad(c=0,1,2,3),$$
where $\sigma_3=\operatorname{sign}(a_{u+1}-a_{v+1})$. The pair $\{c+3u,c+3v\}$ ($c=0,1,2$) is concordant iff $\sigma_c=\sigma_{c+1}$. If $\sigma_0=\sigma_3$, the three steps cannot all be sign changes, so at least one of the three pairs is concordant. Hence
$$\#\{\text{concordant pairs}\}\ge\#\big\{\{u,v\}:(a_u-a_v)(a_{u+1}-a_{v+1})>0\big\}.$$

**Lemma.** For distinct reals $a_u$ ($u\in\mathbb Z/n$), the number of pairs $\{u,v\}$ with $(a_u-a_v)(a_{u+1}-a_{v+1})>0$ ("good" pairs) is at least $\lfloor\frac{n-1}2\rfloor$.

*Proof.* For $1\le m\le\frac n2$ let $\tau_u=\operatorname{sign}(a_{u+m}-a_u)$, $u\in\mathbb Z/n$. The pair $\{u,u+m\}$ is good iff $\tau_u=\tau_{u+1}$. Going once around the cycle the sign changes an even number of times.
- If $m<\frac n2$, each pair at cyclic distance $m$ is $\{u,u+m\}$ for exactly one $u$, so the number of good pairs at distance $m$ is $n-(\text{even})\equiv n\pmod 2$.
  - If $n$ is odd, this is at least $1$ for each $m=1,\dots,\frac{n-1}2$: in total $\ge\frac{n-1}2$.
  - If $n$ is even and $m$ is even: rotate indices so that $a_0$ is the minimum. If no pair at distance $m$ were good, then $\tau_u=(-1)^u\tau_0$; but $\tau_0=\operatorname{sign}(a_m-a_0)=+1$ and $\tau_{n-m}=\operatorname{sign}(a_0-a_{n-m})=-1$, while $n-m$ is even — contradiction. So there is a good pair, and by parity at least $2$.
- If $n=2r$ and $m=r$: the pairs are $\{u,u+r\}$, $u=0,\dots,r-1$, and $\tau_{u+r}=-\tau_u$. Among the $r$ steps $\tau_0\to\tau_1\to\dots\to\tau_r=-\tau_0$ the number of sign changes is odd, so if $r$ is even at least one step is not a change: at least $1$ good pair.

For $n=2r$: the even $m$ with $2\le m<r$ number $\lfloor\frac{r-1}2\rfloor$ and give $\ge2$ each, and $m=r$ gives $\ge1$ when $r$ is even. If $r$ is odd this is $2\cdot\frac{r-1}2=r-1$; if $r$ is even it is $2\left(\frac r2-1\right)+1=r-1$. In all cases we get $\ge\lfloor\frac{n-1}2\rfloor$. $\square$

**Conclusion.**
$$\#\text{self-intersections}\le3\binom n2-\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}2\right\rfloor=\begin{cases}\frac32n^2-2n+\frac12,&n\text{ odd},\\[2pt]\frac32n^2-2n+1,&n\text{ even},\end{cases}$$
which is at most $\frac32n^2-2n+1$. ∎

imc-2014-06.title: Counting small terms
imc-2014-06.body:
Choose $n_0$ such that $d_n(a_n)\ne0$ for all $n\ge n_0$. For such $n$, $a_n$ has a nonzero digit in the $10^{n-1}$ place, so $a_n\ge10^{n-1}$.

Let $N\ge n_0$. If $m>N$, then $a_m\ge10^{m-1}\ge10^N$. So among all terms of the sequence, only $a_1,\dots,a_N$ can lie in $\{1,2,\dots,10^N-1\}$. Hence at least $10^N-1-N$ of these numbers do not occur in the sequence. Since $10^N-1-N\to\infty$, infinitely many positive integers do not occur. ∎

imc-2014-06.title: Cantor's diagonal argument
imc-2014-06.body:
Let $n_0$ be such that $d_n(a_n)\ne0$ for $n\ge n_0$. Define digits $g_n=2$ if $d_n(a_n)=1$ and $g_n=1$ otherwise; so $g_n\ne d_n(a_n)$ and $g_n\ne0$. Let
$$x_k=\sum_{n=1}^kg_n10^{n-1}\qquad(k\ge1).$$
These are strictly increasing ($x_{k+1}\ge10^k>x_k$), hence distinct. We claim $x_k\ne a_n$ for all $k\ge n_0$ and all $n$:
- if $n\le k$, then $d_n(x_k)=g_n\ne d_n(a_n)$;
- if $n>k\ge n_0$, then $d_n(x_k)=0\ne d_n(a_n)$.

So $x_{n_0},x_{n_0+1},\dots$ are infinitely many positive integers missing from the sequence. ∎

imc-2014-07.title: Trace of $A^2$
imc-2014-07.body:
The eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are real, so both sides are real. Since $\operatorname{tr}A=\sum a_{ii}=\sum\lambda_i$,
$$\sum_ia_{ii}^2+2\sum_{i<j}a_{ii}a_{jj}=\Big(\sum_ia_{ii}\Big)^2=\Big(\sum_i\lambda_i\Big)^2=\sum_i\lambda_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}\lambda_i\lambda_j .$$
Hence the inequality is equivalent to
$$\sum_ia_{ii}^2\le\sum_i\lambda_i^2 .$$
The matrix $A^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i^2$, and since $A$ is symmetric,
$$\sum_i\lambda_i^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=\operatorname{tr}(A^TA)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=\sum_ia_{ii}^2+\sum_{i\ne j}a_{ij}^2\ \ge\ \sum_ia_{ii}^2 .$$
This proves the inequality, with equality iff $\sum_{i\ne j}a_{ij}^2=0$, i.e. iff all off-diagonal entries vanish.

**Answer:** equality holds exactly for diagonal matrices. ∎

imc-2014-08.title: An integral representation
imc-2014-08.body:
For $x>0$,
$$f(x)=\frac{\sin x}x=\int_0^1\cos(xt)\,dt .$$
The integrand is smooth in $(x,t)$ and $t$ ranges over a compact interval, so we may differentiate under the integral sign:
$$f^{(n)}(x)=\int_0^1t^n\cos\!\Big(xt+\frac{n\pi}2\Big)\,dt,$$
using $\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\cos(xt)=t^n\cos(xt+\frac{n\pi}2)$. Hence
$$\left|f^{(n)}(x)\right|\le\int_0^1t^n\left|\cos\!\Big(xt+\frac{n\pi}2\Big)\right|dt\le\int_0^1t^n\,dt=\frac1{n+1}.$$
The second inequality is strict: the function $t^n\big(1-|\cos(xt+\frac{n\pi}2)|\big)$ is continuous, nonnegative, and positive except at finitely many $t\in[0,1]$ (where $xt+\frac{n\pi}2\in\pi\mathbb Z$, or $t=0$), so its integral is positive. Therefore $|f^{(n)}(x)|<\frac1{n+1}$. ∎

imc-2014-08.title: A monotone auxiliary function
imc-2014-08.body:
Extend $f$ by $f(0)=1$; then $f(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kx^{2k}}{(2k+1)!}$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$. By Leibniz's rule applied to $xf(x)=\sin x$,
$$(n+1)f^{(n)}(x)+xf^{(n+1)}(x)=\sin^{(n+1)}(x).$$
Let $g_\pm(x)=x^{n+1}\Big(f^{(n)}(x)\mp\frac1{n+1}\Big)$. Then $g_\pm(0)=0$ and
$$g_\pm'(x)=x^n\Big((n+1)f^{(n)}(x)+xf^{(n+1)}(x)\mp1\Big)=x^n\Big(\sin^{(n+1)}(x)\mp1\Big).$$
Since $\sin^{(n+1)}=\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$ has absolute value $\le1$, with equality only at isolated points, $g_+'\le0$ and $g_-'\ge0$ on $(0,\infty)$, and neither vanishes identically on any interval. Hence for $x>0$: $g_+(x)=\int_0^xg_+'<0$ and $g_-(x)>0$, i.e.
$$-\frac1{n+1}<f^{(n)}(x)<\frac1{n+1}.$$
∎

imc-2014-09.title: Tight hyperplanes in a minimal set
imc-2014-09.body:
A hyperplane *misses* a point if the point is not on it. $S$ is $k$-generic iff every hyperplane misses at least $k$ points of $S$.

**$n=1$.** Hyperplanes are points. $S\subset\mathbb R$ is $k$-generic iff $|S\setminus\{p\}|\ge k$ for every $p$, i.e. iff $|S|\ge k+1$. So any $k+1$ points of a $k$-generic set form a $k$-generic subset, and smaller sets are never $k$-generic: $d(k,1)=k+1$.

**$k=1$.** $S$ is $1$-generic iff it lies in no hyperplane, i.e. it affinely spans $\mathbb R^n$. Such a set contains $n+1$ affinely independent points, which again span; and at most $n$ points always lie in a hyperplane. So $d(1,n)=n+1$.

From now on $k,n\ge2$; we show $d(k,n)=kn$.

**The example.** Let $E$ consist of $k$ distinct nonzero points on each coordinate axis ($kn$ points). Let $H$ be a hyperplane.
- If $0\in H$, then $H$ is a linear hyperplane and misses some basis vector $e_j$; then it misses all $k$ chosen points of axis $j$.
- If $0\notin H$, each axis meets $H$ in at most one point, so $H$ contains at most $n$ points of $E$ and misses at least $n(k-1)\ge k$ of them, since $(n-1)(k-1)\ge1$.

So $E$ is $k$-generic. If a point of axis $j$ is removed, the hyperplane $x_j=0$ misses only $k-1$ of the remaining points. So no proper subset of $E$ is $k$-generic, and $d(k,n)\ge kn$. The same argument works in any affine coordinate system.

**Upper bound.** Let $S$ be $k$-generic and let $S'\subseteq S$ be a $k$-generic subset that is minimal under inclusion. We show $|S'|\le kn$.

Call a hyperplane *tight* if it misses exactly $k$ points of $S'$. For $p\in S'$, $S'\setminus\{p\}$ is not $k$-generic, so some hyperplane $H$ misses at most $k-1$ points of $S'\setminus\{p\}$; since $H$ misses at least $k$ points of $S'$, $H$ misses $p$ and is tight. **Every point of $S'$ is missed by a tight hyperplane.**

Suppose $|S'|\ge kn+1$. Build tight hyperplanes $H_1,\dots,H_n$: let $L_0=\mathbb R^n$ and $U_0=S'$. At step $t$ ($1\le t\le n$), $U_{t-1}=S'\cap L_{t-1}$ is nonempty (see below); pick $p\in U_{t-1}$ and a tight $H_t$ missing $p$, and set $L_t=L_{t-1}\cap H_t$, $U_t=S'\cap L_t$. Since $p\in L_{t-1}\setminus H_t$, the flat $L_{t-1}$ is not contained in $H_t$, so $L_t$ is empty or has dimension one less. Each step removes at most $k$ points ($H_t$ is tight), so $|U_t|\ge|S'|-kt\ge1$ for $t\le n$; thus $L_t\ne\emptyset$ and $\dim L_t=n-t$. In the end $L_n=H_1\cap\dots\cap H_n=\{O\}$ with $O\in S'$, and the normals of $H_1,\dots,H_n$ are linearly independent. Choose affine coordinates with origin $O$ in which $H_i=\{x_i=0\}$.

Every point of $S'$ other than $O$ is missed by some $H_i$, so
$$|S'|\le1+\sum_{i=1}^n|S'\setminus H_i|=1+kn .$$
Hence $|S'|=kn+1$ and the sets $S'\setminus H_i$ are pairwise disjoint: each $P\in S'\setminus\{O\}$ lies outside exactly one $H_i$ and on all the others, i.e. on the $x_i$-axis. So $S'\setminus\{O\}$ consists of exactly $k$ nonzero points on each coordinate axis — the example $E$ — which is $k$-generic. This contradicts the minimality of $S'$. Therefore $|S'|\le kn$.

**Answer:** $d(k,n)=kn$ for $k,n>1$, and $d(k,n)=k+n$ if $k=1$ or $n=1$. ∎

imc-2014-10.title: Relabel, count fixed points, use the derangement recursion
imc-2014-10.body:
Put $D_0=1$. Recall $D_{m+1}=m(D_m+D_{m-1})$ for $m\ge1$. Indeed, let $\pi$ be a derangement of $\{1,\dots,m+1\}$ and $i=\pi(m+1)\le m$ ($m$ choices). If $\pi(i)=m+1$, deleting $i$ and $m+1$ leaves a derangement of $m-1$ elements ($D_{m-1}$ ways). Otherwise let $j=\pi^{-1}(m+1)\ne i$ and define $\pi'$ on $\{1,\dots,m\}$ by $\pi'(j)=i$ and $\pi'(x)=\pi(x)$ for $x\ne j$; this is a derangement of $\{1,\dots,m\}$ (as $j\ne i$), and conversely every derangement $\pi'$ of $\{1,\dots,m\}$ arises exactly once (put $j=\pi'^{-1}(i)$, $\pi(j)=m+1$, $\pi(m+1)=i$). So this case gives $D_m$ ways, and
$$\frac{D_{m+1}}{m}=D_m+D_{m-1}\qquad(m\ge1).$$

**Step 1: $\Delta(n,k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kjD_{n-k-j}$.** In a permutation counted by $\Delta(n,k)$, positions $1,\dots,k$ carry the values $k+1,\dots,2k$ (allowed since $k+i\ne i$ and $2k\le n$). The remaining positions $P=\{k+1,\dots,n\}$ carry the values $V=\{1,\dots,k\}\cup\{2k+1,\dots,n\}$ bijectively, subject to $x_j\ne j$ for $j\in P$. Identify $V$ with $P$ via $\varphi(v)=v+k$ for $v\le k$ and $\varphi(v)=v$ for $v\ge2k+1$, and let $y_j=\varphi(x_j)$; then $y$ is a permutation of $P$, and $x\leftrightarrow y$ is a bijection. The conditions become:
- for $j\in\{2k+1,\dots,n\}$: $x_j\ne j\iff y_j\ne j$ ($\varphi$ fixes these values);
- for $j\in\{k+1,\dots,2k\}$: $x_j\ne j$ holds automatically ($j\notin V$), and $y_j=j$ is allowed.

So $\Delta(n,k)$ is the number of permutations of the $(n-k)$-element set $P$ whose fixed points all lie in the $k$-element subset $\{k+1,\dots,2k\}$. Sorting by the set of fixed points (choose $j$ of the $k$ special elements to be fixed, derange the other $n-k-j$):
$$\Delta(n,k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom kjD_{n-k-j}.$$

**Step 2: the formula.** For $0\le i\le k-1$, $m=n-k-i\ge n-2k+1\ge1$, so $\frac{D_{(n+1)-(k+i)}}{n-(k+i)}=D_{n-k-i}+D_{n-k-i-1}$. Hence
$$\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}i\frac{D_{n+1-k-i}}{n-k-i}=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{i}D_{n-k-i}+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\binom{k-1}{i-1}D_{n-k-i}=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom kjD_{n-k-j}$$
by Pascal's rule $\binom{k-1}j+\binom{k-1}{j-1}=\binom kj$. By Step 1 this equals $\Delta(n,k)$. ∎
